assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED made a superconducting artificial atom strongly coupled to a single microwave photon in a resonator, giving dispersive readout, controlled entanglement and the architecture of today's superconducting processors. It is a clean new regime of light-matter physics (strong coupling in a solid-state circuit) with decisive experiments and a proven platform. As a theorist embedded in this community I find the physical clarity high, but I am aware of my proximity to the field.
assessment.attribution: The 2004 theory (Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin, Schoelkopf) and the Yale experiment (Wallraff et al., Nature 2004) are tightly linked; Schoelkopf (experiment), Girvin and Blais (theory) are a natural trio. Wallraff, an experimental first author, and others are not in the supplied credited names, so the credit is not fully exhaustive.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced and extended across many laboratories for two decades, with transmon and error-correction demonstrations built on it. The 2025 prize recognised macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, so timing is arguably right now, but the committee must avoid overlap with that citation.
uncertainties: Whether the 2025 award for circuit macroscopic quantum effects makes a second superconducting-circuit prize premature
Credit split between the 2004 theory proposal and experiment, with Wallraff and Nakamura-type contributions outside the supplied names
My own conflict of interest as WACQT director and close colleague of groups in this area

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Topological insulators opened a new class of quantum matter with protected edge or surface states, from the theoretical quantum spin Hall proposal to the HgTe experiment. Originality and lasting influence are very high, with a deep link to the 2016 topology prize but a distinct discovery.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the decisive theoretical proposal; Molenkamp's group delivered the first experimental realisation in HgTe wells (with Zhang's theory prediction of the HgTe case). Zhang, Bernevig and Hughes are not among the credited names here, so the allocation is not complete. The 3D topological insulator work (Hasan, Moore, Balents, Fu) also lies outside this candidate.
assessment.maturity: Many independent confirmations, including ARPES and transport, and a stable interpretation. Recognition is timely, with roughly two decades of impact.
uncertainties: Prize configuration is contested between 2D and 3D topological insulator contributions
Zhang's HgTe prediction and Hasan's 3D experiments are not in the supplied credited names
Overlap with the 2016 topological phases prize

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength idea, reached 10^-18 systematic uncertainty and enable tests of fundamental physics and relativistic geodesy. This is a precision-measurement breakthrough with clear physical content and a vivid scientific signal.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and demonstrated the first clock; Ye drove the highest-precision realisations and the clock-comparison and many-body physics. Hall and Hänsch were already recognised for the comb. A two-person award looks fair, though Lemonde, Takamoto and Ludlow would be mentioned.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed across many labs; redefinition of the SI second is under discussion, so recognition is timely and not premature.
uncertainties: Redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so the practical culmination is incomplete
Whether the committee sees this as an enabling technology on top of the 2005 prize rather than a new discovery

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cold atoms in optical lattices realise Hubbard models with tunable parameters, including the superfluid to Mott insulator transition and single-site quantum gas microscopy. This created a lasting platform for quantum simulation of many-body physics and links well with my interest in controllable quantum devices.
assessment.attribution: Jaksch, Zoller and co-workers made the theory proposal; Greiner, Bloch and Hänsch demonstrated the Mott transition; Bloch and Greiner developed gas microscopes; Esslinger realised the fermionic Mott insulator. Allocation is complicated with four credited names and the choice of three is judgmental. Zoller's other contributions overlap with B019 and B051.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with many independent laboratories and results. Quantum advantage claims for simulation remain partly open, but the discovery-level results are firmly established.
uncertainties: Allocation among Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger and Zoller, plus omitted Jaksch and Hänsch
Overlap in Zoller credit with other quantum-simulation candidates
How much of the impact is technique rather than a single discovery

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution turned fundamental quantum features (no cloning, entanglement and Bell tests) into a protocol for provably secure communication, defining a field. The conceptual originality is high and is closely tied to experimental tests of quantum foundations.
assessment.attribution: BB84 (Bennett and Brassard) and E91 (Ekert) are the canonical protocols; the credit trio is natural. Wiesner's conjugate coding and Zeilinger's and Gisin's experimental demonstrations lie outside the supplied names. Note the 2022 prize already recognised entanglement experiments, so some adjacency.
assessment.maturity: Long experimental record, including satellite demonstrations; practical security loopholes are known, but the principle is well established.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 prize on Bell tests and quantum information science
Whether the discovery is a theory of protocols more than of physical phenomena
Wiesner and experimentalists are omitted from the credit

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The theoretical prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle and the 2018 observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity opened the field of moiré quantum matter, an unusually rich and controllable platform with a large literature.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the key prediction; Jarillo-Herrero's group made the decisive 2018 experiments (Cao et al., with Kim, Fu and collaborators). A clear theory plus experiment trio exists, although Yuan Cao as first author and others' contributions are outside the allowed names.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by many groups, although the nature of the superconductivity and the correlated phases is still debated. The field may be a few years early for a prize.
uncertainties: Mechanism of superconductivity remains unsettled
Sample dependence and twist-angle disorder are still issues
Timeliness: the interpretation is still evolving

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The light-matter quantum interface and quantum repeater architecture established how photons and atomic ensembles or single atoms can transfer quantum states, which is the basis of quantum networks. Conceptually valuable and a bridge between quantum optics and information.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller made the theory proposals for quantum state transfer and networks, and Kimble led the experiments on cavity QED and network nodes. Others such as Duan, Lukin, Polzik and Rempe have important contributions outside the supplied names.
assessment.maturity: Quantum networks are at an early stage. Elementary links are demonstrated, but scalable networks are still ahead, so recognition may be premature.
uncertainties: Technology is still prototypical and no scalable network has been shown
Credit overlaps with other candidates involving Zoller and Cirac and with the 2012 and 2022 prizes
Many leading experimentalists are not in the credited names

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed states of light beat the standard quantum limit in interferometry, and their use in gravitational-wave detectors has made them practically important. A clear quantum-optical principle with a spectacular real-world demonstration in LIGO and Virgo.
assessment.attribution: Caves provided the 1981 theory; Kimble's group provided the first strong experimental squeezing; Schnabel and others carried it to gravitational-wave detectors. Slusher, Walls, Wu, McClelland and Lam are outside the credited names, so a fair allocation is difficult to defend.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed and deployed in LIGO since 2011, but the credit disputes make timing complex.
uncertainties: Large number of key contributors who are not in the credited names
Possible overlap with the 2017 gravitational-wave prize
Whether the committee views this as a method rather than a discovery
